                                              LINEAR GROUPS - MALCEV’S THEOREM AND SELBERG’S
                                                                  LEMMA

                                                                                  BOGDAN NICA
arXiv:1306.2385v1 [math.GR] 10 Jun 2013




                                                 Abstract. These notes give an account of two fundamental facts concerning finitely
                                                 generated linear groups: Malcev’s theorem on residual finiteness, and Selberg’s lemma
                                                 on virtual torsion-freeness.




                                                                                  Introduction
                                             A group is linear if it is (isomorphic to) a subgroup of GLn (K), where K is a field.
                                          If we want to specify the field, we say that the group is linear over K. The following
                                          theorems are fundamental, at least from the perspective of combinatorial group theory.
                                          Theorem (Malcev 1940). A finitely generated linear group is residually finite.
                                          Theorem (Selberg 1960). A finitely generated linear group over a field of zero charac-
                                          teristic is virtually torsion-free.
                                             A group is residually finite if its elements are distinguished by the finite quotients
                                          of the group, i.e., if each non-trivial element of the group remains non-trivial in a finite
                                          quotient. A group is virtually torsion-free if some finite-index subgroup is torsion-
                                          free. As a matter of further terminology, Selberg’s theorem is usually referred to as
                                          Selberg’s lemma, and Malcev is alternatively transliterated as Mal’cev or Maltsev.
                                          Contents. The main body of this text has three sections. In the first one we discuss
                                          residual finiteness and virtual torsion-freeness, with emphasis on their relation to a
                                          third property - roughly speaking, a “p-adic” refinement of residual finiteness. The
                                          main theorem we are actually interested in, due to Platonov (1968), gives such refined
                                          residual properties for finitely generated linear groups. Both Malcev’s theorem and
                                          Selberg’s lemma are consequences of this more powerful, but lesser known, theorem of
                                          Platonov. The second section is devoted to SLn (Z). This example is too important,
                                          too interesting, too much fun to receive anything less than a scenic analysis. In the last
                                          section we return to a proof of Platonov’s theorem.
                                          Comments. Besides the Russian original [2], the only other source in the literature for
                                          Platonov’s theorem that I am aware of is the account of Wehrfritz in [5, Chapter 4].
                                          The proof presented herein is, I think, considerably simpler. It is mainly influenced by
                                          the discussion of Malcev’s theorem in the lecture notes by Stallings [4], and it is quite
                                          similar to Platonov’s own arguments in [2].
                                             An alternative road to Selberg’s lemma is to use valuations. This is the approach
                                          taken by Cassels in Local fields (Cambridge University Press 1986), and by Ratcliffe in
                                          Foundations of hyperbolic manifolds (2nd edition, Springer 2006).
                                            Date: June 2013.

  I thank, in chronological order, Andy Putman for a useful answer via mathoverflow.net,
Jean-François Planchat for a careful reading and constructive comments, and Vadim
Alekseev for a translation of Platonov’s article.
Convention. In this text, rings are commutative and unital.

                 1. Virtual and residual properties of groups
   Virtual torsion-freeness and residual finiteness are instances of the following terminol-
ogy. Let P be a group-theoretic property. A group is virtually P if it has a finite-index
subgroup enjoying P. A group is residually P if each non-trivial element of the group
remains non-trivial in some quotient group enjoying P. The virtually P groups and the
residually P groups contain the P groups. It may certainly happen that a property is
virtually stable (e.g., finiteness) or residually stable (e.g., torsion-freeness).
   Besides virtual torsion-freeness and residual finiteness, we are interested in the hybrid
notion of virtual residual p-finiteness where p is a prime. This is obtained by
residualizing the property of being a finite p-group, followed by the virtual extension.
The notion of virtual residual p-finiteness has, in fact, the leading role in this account
for it relates both to residual finiteness and to virtual torsion-freeness.
Lemma 1.1 (“Going down”). If P is inherited by subgroups, then both virtually P and
residually P are inherited by subgroups. In particular, virtual torsion-freeness, residual
finiteness, and virtual residual p-finiteness are inherited by subgroups.
Lemma 1.2 (“Going up”). Virtually P passes to finite-index supergroups. In partic-
ular, both virtual torsion-freeness and virtual residual p-finiteness pass to finite-index
supergroups. Residual finiteness passes to finite-index supergroups.
   Observe that residual p-finiteness, just like torsion-freeness, is not virtually stable.
Residual finiteness does pass to finite-index supergroups because of the following equiv-
alent description: a group is residually finite if and only if every non-trivial element lies
outside of a finite-index subgroup.
   Residual p-finiteness trivially implies residual finiteness. Going up, we obtain:
Proposition 1.3. Virtual residual p-finiteness for some prime p implies residual finite-
ness.
   On the other hand, residual p-finiteness imposes torsion restrictions. Namely, in a
residually p-finite group, the order of a torsion element must be a p-th power. Hence,
if a group is residually p-finite and residually q-finite for two different primes p and q,
then it is torsion-free. Virtualizing this statement, we obtain:
Proposition 1.4. Virtual residual p-finiteness and virtual residual q-finiteness for two
different primes p and q imply virtual torsion-freeness.
  In light of Propositions 1.3 and 1.4, we see that Malcev’s theorem and Selberg’s
lemma are consequences of the following:
Theorem (Platonov 1968). Let G be a finitely generated linear group over a field K.
If char K = 0, then G is virtually residually p-finite for all but finitely many primes p.
If char K = p, then G is virtually residually p-finite.
                LINEAR GROUPS - MALCEV’S THEOREM AND SELBERG’S LEMMA                           3

                                      2. Essellennzee
  In this section we examine SLn (Z), where n ≥ 2. We start with a most familiar fact.
Proposition 2.1. SLn (Z) is generated by the elementary matrices {1n + eij : i 6= j}.
Proof. In general, if A is a euclidean domain then SLn (A) is generated by the elementary
matrices {1n + a · eij : a ∈ A, i 6= j}. The first step is to turn any matrix in SLn (A)
into a diagonal one via elementary operations. Using division with remainder, and the
euclidean map on A as a way of measuring the decrease in complexity, we can insure
that a single non-zero entry, say a, remains in the first row. Column swapping brings a
in position (1, 1), and row reductions using the invertible a turn all other entries in the
first column to 0. Now repeat this procedure for the remaining (n − 1) × (n − 1) block.
The second step is to bring a diagonal matrix of determinant 1 to the identity matrix
1n via elementary operations. This is done using the transition
              a 0         a a              1      a              1 a           1 0
                                                                              
                                                                                    .
              0 b         0 b          (a−1 − 1)b b              0 ab          0 ab
Finally, if the additive group of A is generated by {a1 , . . . , ak }, then the corresponding
matrices {1n + a1 · eij , . . . , 1n + ak · eij : i 6= j} generate all the elementary matrices. 

  Let N be a positive integer. Reduction modulo N defines a group homomorphism
SLn (Z) → SLn (Z/N ), which enjoys the following remarkable property:
Lemma 2.2. The congruence homomorphism SLn (Z) → SLn (Z/N ) is onto.
Proof. Since SLn (Z) is generated by the elementary matrices, and the elementary ma-
trices are mapped to the elementary matrices by the congruence homomorphism, its
surjectivity is equivalent to the elementary generation of SLn (Z/N ). The Chinese Re-
                                                            si
mainder Theorem provides     a decomposition       ≃        i into local rings, mirroring
                                                     Q
                           Q si
                                               Z/N      Z/p
the decomposition N = pi into primes. Direct products preserve elementary gen-
eration, and we now show that it holds over local rings. This is actually easier than
elementary generation for euclidean domains. Let A be a local ring and pick a matrix in
SLn (A). Some first-row entry is not in π, the maximal ideal of A, so it is invertible in A.
Column swapping brings this element in the (1, 1)-position, and then the first row and
the first column can be cleared. The rest goes as in the proof of Proposition 2.1.        

  The kernel of the congruence homomorphism
                                                   
         Γ(N ) := ker SLn (Z) → SLn (Z/N ) = X ∈ SLn (Z) : X ≡ 1n mod N
is the principal congruence subgroup of level N . In particular, Γ(1) = SLn (Z).
   The principal congruence subgroups are normal, finite-index subgroups of SLn (Z).
The following lemma provides the formula for their index.

Next, we find the size of SLn (Z/pk ). Consider again the general case of a local ring A
with maximal ideal π. The congruence map GLn (A) → GLn (A/π) is onto: any lift to
A of a matrix in GLn (A/π) has determinant not in π, i.e., invertible in A. Furthermore,
the kernel of the congruence map GLn (A) → GLn (A/π) is 1n + Mn (π) since a matrix
congruent to 1n modulo π has determinant in 1 + π, hence invertible in A. Thus, if A
is also finite, then

Finally, the size of SLn (Z/N ) is obtained by multiplying the above formula over the
prime decomposition of N .                                                         
   Bass - Lazard - Serre (Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 1964) and Mennicke (Ann. Math.
1965) have shown that, for n ≥ 3, every finite-index subgroup of SLn (Z) contains some
principal congruence subgroup. This Congruence Subgroup Property is definitely not
true for n = 2. The first one to state this failure was Klein (1880), and proofs were
subsequently provided by Fricke (1886) and Pick (1886). It is in fact known by now that
it is an exceptional feature for a finite-index subgroup of SL2 (Z) to contain a principal
congruence subgroup.
   The principal congruence subgroups are organized according to the divisibility of their
levels: Γ(M ) ⊇ Γ(N ) ⇔ M |N , that is, “to contain is to divide”. This puts the emphasis
on the prime stratum {Γ(p) : p prime}, and on the descending chains {Γ(pk ) : k ≥ 1}
corresponding to each prime p. Observe that ∩p Γ(p) = {1n }, and that ∩k Γ(pk ) = {1n }
for each prime p, meaning that the elements of SLn (Z) can be distinguished both along
the prime stratum, as well as along each descending p-chain. Thus:
Proposition 2.4. SLn (Z) is residually finite.
    Clearly SLn (Z) is not torsion-free. For example,
                                      0 −1              0 −1
                                                         
                                           ,
                                      1 0               1 1
are elements of order 4, respectively 6, in SL2 (Z). However, we have:
Proposition 2.5. SLn (Z) is virtually torsion-free.
    This is an immediate consequence of the following fact, due to Minkowski (1887):
Lemma 2.6. Γ(N ) is torsion-free provided N ≥ 3.
              LINEAR GROUPS - MALCEV’S THEOREM AND SELBERG’S LEMMA                          5

Proof. It suffices to show that Γ(4) and Γ(p), where p ≥ 3 is a prime, are torsion-free.
Let p be any prime, and assume that X ∈ Γ(p) is a non-trivial element having finite
order. Up to replacing X by a power of itself, we may assume that X q = 1n for a prime
q. Then
                                            q         !
                                            X q
                            −q(X − 1n ) =             (X − 1n )i .
                                            i≥2
                                                  i

Let ps , where s ≥ 1, be the highest power of p dividing all the entries of X − 1n . The
left hand side of the displayed identity is divisible by at most ps if q 6= p, and by at most
ps+1 if q = p. The right hand side is divisible by p2s , and even by p2s+1 if q = p ≥ 3.
Hence q = p = 2 and s = 1. The conclusion that p = 2 and s = 1 means that Γ(2) is the
only one in the prime stratum which harbours torsion, and that Γ(4), its successor in
the descending 2-chain, is free of torsion. The conclusion that q = 2 means that torsion
elements in Γ(2) have order a power of 2. As X 2 ∈ Γ(4) whenever X ∈ Γ(2), and Γ(4)
is torsion-free, it follows that non-trivial torsion elements in Γ(2) have order 2.        

   This lemma can be used to control the torsion spectrum - that is, the possible or-
ders of torsion elements - in SLn (Z). Let us illustrate the basic idea in the simplest
case, when n = 2. Given a group homomorphism, the torsion spectra of its domain,
kernel, and range are trivially related by τ (dom) ⊆ τ (ker) · τ (ran). In the case of a con-
gruence homomorphism, this reads as τ (SL2 (Z)) ⊆ τ (Γ(N )) · τ (SL2 (Z/N )). If N = 3
then τ (Γ(3)) = {1}, and it can be checked that τ (SL2 (Z/3)) = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}. Some-
what easier, in fact, is to let N = 2: then τ (Γ(2)) = {1, 2}, and it is immediate that
τ (SL2 (Z/2)) = {1, 2, 3}. We conclude that τ (SL2 (Z)) ⊆ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}. Equality holds,
actually, since there are elements of order 4 and 6 in SL2 (Z).
   The presence of a torsion element with composite order, namely 6, implies that
SLn (Z) is not residually p-finite for any prime p. As with torsion-freeness, this is easily
remedied by passing to a finite-index subgroup:
Proposition 2.7. SLn (Z) is virtually residually p-finite for each prime p.
  More precisely, we show:
Lemma 2.8. Γ(N ) is residually p-finite for each prime p dividing N .
Proof. It suffices to prove that, for each prime p, Γ(p) is residually p-finite. To that
end, we claim that each successive quotient Γ(pk )/Γ(pk+1 ) in the descending chain
{Γ(pk ) : k ≥ 1} is a p-group. This is seen most directly by observing that each element
in Γ(pk )/Γ(pk+1 ) has order p: for any matrix 1n + pk X ∈ Γ(pk ) we have
                                            p  !
                              k   p
                                            X p ki
                      (1n + p X) = 1n +               p X i ∈ Γ(pk+1 ).
                                            i=1
                                                  i

   Another way is to use the formula for the index (Lemma 2.3), which yields that
                           2
Γ(pk )/Γ(pk+1 ) has size pn −1 .
   A third, more involved argument shows that each successive quotient Γ(pk )/Γ(pk+1 )
                            2
is isomorphic to (Z/p, +)n −1 . Start by noting that, for any matrix 1n + pk X ∈ Γ(pk ),
6                                        BOGDAN NICA

we have 1 = det(1n + pk X) = 1 + pk tr(X) mod p2k ; in particular, p divides tr(X). Let
sln (Z/p) denote the additive group of traceless n × n matrices over Z/p. Then the map
                    φk : Γ(pk ) → sln (Z/p),    φk (1n + pk X) = X mod p
is well-defined. Firstly, φk is ahomomorphism: for 1n + pk X and 1n + pk Y in Γ(pk ) we
have φk (1n + pk X)(1n + pk Y ) = X + Y + pk XY mod p = X + Y mod p. Secondly, the
kernel of φk is Γ(pk+1 ). Thirdly, we claim that φk is onto. The target group sln (Z/p)
is generated by the n2 − n off-diagonal matrix units {eij : 1 ≤ i 6= j ≤ n} together with
the n − 1 diagonal differences {eii − ei+1 i+1 : 1 ≤ i ≤ n − 1}. It is immediate that the
off-diagonal matrix units are in the image of φk , as φk (1n + pk eij ) = eij for i 6= j. To
obtain the diagonal differences, consider an n × n matrix having the 2 × 2-block
                                                        !
                                        1 + pk   pk
                                         −p k  1 − pk
on the diagonal, all the other non-zero entries being 1’s along the remaining diagonal
slots. This is a matrix in Γ(pk ) which is mapped by φk to eii − ei+1 i+1 + ei i+1 − ei+1 i .
As ei i+1 and ei+1 i are in the image of φk , the same is true for eii − ei+1 i+1 .      
Remark 2.9. Scratch most properties of SLn (Z) and you will find a great discrepancy
between SL2 (Z) and SLn≥3 (Z) lurking underneath. For the discussion at hand, the
difference turns out to be the following: SL2 (Z) admits finite-index subgroups which
are residually p-finite for all primes p, whereas in SLn≥3 (Z) every finite-index subgroup
is residually p-finite for only finitely many primes p. The question which clarifies and
sharpens this contrast is whether principal congruence subgroups can be residually p-
finite for a prime p not dividing the level.
   In SL2 (Z), the answer is that Γ(2) is residually p-finite for p = 2 only, but Γ(N ) with
N ≥ 3 is residually p-finite for all primes p. The exceptional case is due to the 2-torsion
in Γ(2). In the higher level case there is no torsion. Now a torsion-free subgroup of
SL2 (Z) is free, since SL2 (Z) acts on a tree with finite vertex stabilizers and without
inversion (see I.§4 of Serre’s Trees, Springer 1980). Thus Γ(N ) with N ≥ 3 is free. We
may then use mutual abstract embeddings to conclude that Γ(N ) with N ≥ 3, in fact
every free group, is residually p-finite for all primes p.
   In SLn≥3 (Z), the answer is that Γ(N ) is residually p-finite if and only if p divides N .
Once we know this, the Congruence Subgroup Property will imply that each finite-index
subgroup of SLn≥3 (Z) is residually p-finite for only finitely many primes p. Now let us
justify the answer, specifically the forward implication. The proof hinges on computing
the abelianization of Γ(N ), and this is essentially due to Lee and Szczarba (Invent.
Math. 1976). As in the proof of Lemma 2.8, there is a well-defined homomorphism
                       Γ(N ) → sln (Z/N ),     1n + N X 7→ X mod N
                                                                                  2
which is furthermore onto. Thus Γ(N )/Γ(N 2 ) ≃ sln (Z/N ) ≃ (Z/N, +)n −1 , and the
commutator subgroup [Γ(N ), Γ(N )] is contained in Γ(N 2 ). On the other hand, we have
1n + N 2 eik = [1n + N eij , 1n + N ejk ] ∈ [Γ(N ), Γ(N )] for distinct i, j, k. At this point we
use the fact that the principal congruence subgroup of level M is normally generated
by {1n + M eij : i 6= j}, the M -th powers of the elementary matrices. This is what
Mennicke actually proved in his approach to the Congruence Subgroup Property. As
              LINEAR GROUPS - MALCEV’S THEOREM AND SELBERG’S LEMMA                          7

pointed out soon after by Bass - Milnor - Serre (Publ. Math. IHES 1967), this fact is
equivalent to the Congruence Subgroup Property. It follows that Γ(N 2 ) is contained
in [Γ(N ), Γ(N )], by the normality of Γ(N ). Summarizing, [Γ(N ), Γ(N )] = Γ(N 2 ), so
                                               2
that the abelianization of Γ(N ) is (Z/N, +)n −1 . Finally, if Γ(N ) maps onto a non-
trivial finite p-group then the abelianization of Γ(N ) maps onto the corresponding
abelianization, which is a non-trivial p-group, and we conclude that p divides N .


                          3. Proof of Platonov’s theorem
   Let G be a finitely generated linear group over a field K, say G ≤ GLn (K). In K,
consider the subring A generated by the multiplicative identity 1 and the matrix entries
of a finite, symmetric set of generators for G. Thus A is a finitely generated domain,
and G ≤ GLn (A). Platonov’s theorem is then a consequence of the following:

Theorem 3.1. Let A be a finitely generated domain. If char A = 0, then GLn (A)
is virtually residually p-finite for all but finitely many primes p. If char A = p, then
GLn (A) is virtually residually p-finite.

   The proof of Theorem 3.1 is a straightforward variation on the example of SLn (Z),
as soon as we know the following facts:

Lemma 3.2. Let A be a finitely generated domain. Then the following hold:
      i. A is noetherian.
     ii. ∩k I k = 0 for any ideal I 6= A.
    iii. If A is a field, then A is finite.
    iv. The intersection of maximal ideals of A is 0.
     v. If char A = 0, then only finitely many primes p = p · 1 are invertible in A.

  Let us postpone the proof of Lemma 3.2 for the moment, and see how to obtain
Theorem 3.1. The principal congruence subgroup of GLn (A) corresponding to an ideal
I of A is defined by
                                                               
                           Γ(I) = ker GLn (A) → GLn (A/I) .

If π is a maximal ideal then A/π is a finite field, by 3.2 iii, so Γ(π) has finite index in
GLn (A). Also ∩π Γ(π) = {1n } as π runs over the maximal ideals of A, by 3.2 iv. This
shows that GLn (A) is residually finite, thereby proving Malcev’s theorem.
   We claim that π k /π k+1 is finite for each k ≥ 1. In general, if M is an R-module which
is annihilated by an ideal I – in the sense that IM = 0 – then M is also an R/I-module
in a natural way: namely, define r · m := r · m for r ∈ R and m ∈ M . Furthermore, if
M is finitely generated as an R-module then M is finitely generated as an R/I-module.
In the case at hand, the A-module π k is finitely generated since A is noetherian, so the
A-module π k /π k+1 is also finitely generated. Therefore π k /π k+1 is finite dimensional
as an A/π-module. As A/π is finite, π k /π k+1 is finite as well.
   The ring A/π k is finite for each k ≥ 1, so each Γ(π k ) has finite index in GLn (A). Fur-
thermore, ∩k Γ(π k ) = {1n } by 3.2 ii. (This shows once again that GLn (A) is residually
finite.) Let p be the characteristic of A/π, so p ∈ π. Then Γ(π k )/Γ(π k+1 ) is a p-group:
8                                           BOGDAN NICA

for X ∈ Γ(π k ) we have
                                         p          !
                             p
                                         X p
                           X = 1n +                 (X − 1n )i ∈ Γ(π k+1 ).
                                         i=1
                                                i
To conclude, GLn (A) is virtually residually p-finite for each prime p not invertible in A.
By 3.2 v, this happens for all but finitely many primes p in the zero characteristic case.
In characteristic p, there is only such prime, namely p itself. Theorem 3.1 is proved.
   We now return to the proof of the lemma.
Proof of Lemma 3.2. The first two points are standard: i) follows from the Hilbert Basis
Theorem, and ii) is the Krull Intersection Theorem for domains.
  iii) We use the following fact:
        Let F ⊆ F (u) be a field extension with F (u) finitely generated as a ring.
        Then F ⊆ F (u) is a finite extension and F is finitely generated as a ring.
Here is how we use this fact. Let F be the prime field of A and let a1 , . . . , aN be
generators of A as a ring. Thus A = F (a1 , . . . , aN ). Going down the chain
                      A = F (a1 , . . . , aN ) ⊇ F (a1 , . . . , aN −1 ) ⊇ . . . ⊇ F
we obtain that F ⊆ A is a finite extension, and that F is finitely generated as a ring.
Then F is a finite field, as Q is not finitely generated as a ring, and so A is finite.
   Now here is how we prove the fact. Assume that u is transcendental over F , i.e., F (u)
is the field of rational functions in u. Let P1 /Q1 , . . . , PN Q N
                                                                     /Q generate F (u) as a ring,
where Pi , Qi ∈ F [u]. The multiplicative inverse      of   1+u·      Qi isQa polynomial expression
in the Pi /Qi ’s, which can be written Q        as R/ Qsi i . Therefore Qsi i = (1Q+ u · Qi )R
                                                     Q                                     Q

in F [u]. But this is impossible, since Qsi i is relatively prime to 1 + u · Qi .
   Thus u is algebraic over F . Let X d + α1 X d−1 + · · · + αd be the minimal polynomial
of u over F   . Let also a1 , . . . , aN be ring generators of F (u) = F [u]. We may write
each ai as 0≤m≤d−1 βi,m um , with βi,m ∈ F . We claim that the αj ’s and the βi,m ’s are
             P

ring generators of F . Let c ∈ F . Then c is a polynomial in a1 , . . . , aN over F , hence a
polynomial in u over the subring of F generated by the βi,m ’s, hence a polynomial in
u of degree less than d over the subring of F generated by the αj ’s and the βi,m ’s. By
the linear independence of {1, u, . . . , ud−1 }, the latter polynomial is actually of degree
0. Hence c ends up in the subring of F generated by the αj ’s and the βi,m ’s.
   iv) Let a 6= 0 in A. To find a maximal ideal of A not containing a, we rely on the basic
avoidance: maximal ideals do not contain invertible elements. Consider the localization
A′ = A[1/a]. Let π ′ be a maximal ideal in A′ , so a ∈        / π ′ . The restriction π = π ′ ∩ A is
an ideal in A, and a ∈  / π. We show that π is maximal. The embedding A ֒→ A′ induces
an embedding A/π ֒→ A′ /π ′ . As A′ /π ′ is a field which is finitely generated as a ring, in
follows from iii) that A′ /π ′ is finite field. Therefore the subring A/π is a finite domain,
hence a field as well.
   v) We shall use Noether’s Normalization Theorem, which says the following.
         Let R be a finitely generated algebra over a field F ⊆ R. Then there are
         elements x1 , . . . , xN ∈ R algebraically independent over F such that R
         is integral over F [x1 , . . . , xN ].
   In our case, Z is a subring of A, and A is an integral domain which is finitely generated
as a Z-algebra. Extending to rational scalars, we have that AQ = Q ⊗Z A is a finitely
               LINEAR GROUPS - MALCEV’S THEOREM AND SELBERG’S LEMMA                               9

generated Q-algebra. By the Normalization Theorem, there exist elements x1 , . . . , xN
in AQ which are algebraically independent over Q, and such that AQ is integral over
Q[x1 , . . . , xN ]. Up to replacing each xi by an integral multiple of itself, we may assume
that x1 , . . . , xN are in A. There is some positive m ∈ Z such that each ring generator
of A is integral over Z[1/m][x1 , . . . , xN ]. Thus A[1/m] is integral over the subring
Z[1/m][x1 , . . . , xN ]. If a prime p is invertible in A, then it is also invertible in A[1/m]
while at the same time p ∈ Z[1/m][x1 , . . . , xN ].
   Now we use the following general fact. Let R be a ring which is integral over a subring
S. If s ∈ S is invertible in R, then s is already invertible in S. The proof is easy. Let
r ∈ R with rs = 1. We have r d + s1 r d−1 + · · · + sd−1 r + sd = 0 for some si ∈ S, since r
is integral over S. Multiplying through by sd−1 yields r ∈ S.
   Returning to our proof, we infer that p is invertible in Z[1/m][x1 , . . . , xN ]. By the
algebraic independence of x1 , . . . , xN , it follows that p is actually invertible in Z[1/m].
But only finitely many primes have this property, namely the prime factors of m.             
Remark 3.3. Let A be an infinite, finitely generated domain with char A = p > 0.
   If n ≥ 2 then the p-torsion group (A, +) embeds in GLn (A), and this prevents GLn (A)
from being virtually residually ℓ-finite for any prime ℓ 6= p. So we cannot do any better
in the positive characteristic case of Theorem 3.1.
   Selberg’s lemma fails in positive characteristic for a similar reason. The elementary
group En (A) = h1n +a·eij : a ∈ A, i 6= ji is linear over the fraction field of A, and it fails
to be virtually torsion-free since it contains copies of the infinite torsion group (A, +).
Furthermore, if n ≥ 3 then En (A) is finitely generated. This is due to the commutator
relations [1n + a · eij , 1n + b · ejk ] = 1n + ab · eik for distinct i, j, k, which imply that
En (A) is generated by {1n + a1 · eij , . . . , 1n + aN · eij : i 6= j} whenever a1 , . . . , aN are
ring generators for A. For a concrete example, take A to be the polynomial ring Fp [t],
in which case En (Fp [t]) = SLn (Fp [t]) since Fp [t] is a euclidean domain.
Remark 3.4. Among finitely generated groups, we have the following implications:
      linear ⇒ virtually residually p-finite for some prime p ⇒ residually finite
The first implication, a “p-adic” refinement of Malcev’s theorem, is an immediate con-
sequence of Platonov’s theorem. The second implication is Proposition 1.3. Neither
implication can be reversed, as witnessed by the following examples.
   According to the previous remark, SLn (Fp [t]) for n ≥ 3 is finitely generated and
virtually residually ℓ-finite for ℓ = p only. Therefore SLn (Fp [t]) × SLn (Fq [t]), where
p and q are different primes, is finitely generated, residually finite but not virtually
residually ℓ-finite for any prime ℓ.
   The automorphism group of the free group on n generators, Aut(Fn ), is virtually
residually p-finite for all primes p. Indeed, as we have seen in Remark 2.9, free groups
are residually p-finite for all primes p. Now a theorem of Lubotzky (J. Algebra 1980)
says that Aut(G) is virtually residually p-finite whenever the finitely generated group
G is virtually residually p-finite. This is the “p-adic” analogue of an older, simpler, and
better known theorem of G. Baumslag (J. London Math Soc. 1963) saying that Aut(G)
is residually finite whenever the finitely generated group G is residually finite. On the
other hand, Formanek and Procesi (J. Algebra 1992) have shown that Aut(Fn ) is not
linear for n ≥ 3.
